card_facts.quote: Muscles and ligaments pull up bumps (projections), while joints, vessels, and nerves leave pits, grooves, and holes (depressions).
card_facts.correction: False split. Joints make BOTH kinds of marking: articular projections (head, condyle, facet) and articular depressions (fossa, notch). The manual says 'Projections are usually part of articulating surfaces or serve as attachment sites for muscles or ligaments', and the figure on this very card prints a list titled 'Projections involved in articulations: head, neck, facet, condyle, ramus'. Suggested: 'Projections are mostly muscle/ligament attachment sites or joint surfaces (head, condyle, facet); depressions are joint sockets or passages for vessels and nerves (fossa, groove, foramen).'

card_facts.quote: from the side it looks like a giraffe's head, with the long, down-slanting spinous process as the neck
card_facts.correction: Contradicts the manual's giraffe figure, which is the picture on this card. There the long spinous process is the giraffe's long FACE/snout pointing down, the upward processes are the ears/horns, and the vertebral body is where the neck comes in. The manual calls the whole vertebra 'a giraffe head'. Suggested: 'from the side it looks like a giraffe's head: the long, down-slanting spinous process is the giraffe's long face.'

card_facts.quote: the long spinous process slants steeply down like a giraffe's neck
card_facts.correction: Same mapping error as card 78. In the manual's figure the spinous process is the giraffe's long face/snout, not its neck. Suggested: 'slants steeply down like a giraffe's long face'.

card_facts.quote: packed solid with no open spaces
card_facts.correction: Compact bone is full of microscopic spaces: central and perforating canals, lacunae, canaliculi (cards 22-26 teach them). Suggested: 'densely packed, with none of the large open spaces of spongy bone'.

card_facts.quote: Only the curved plates of the skull cap (like the frontal and parietal) are flat; the complex bones of the face and cranial floor are irregular.
card_facts.correction: Too absolute. Standard classifications (for example Gray's) also count as flat the occipital, which forms much of the cranial floor, and the small facial plates: nasal, lacrimal, vomer. The irregular ones are the sphenoid, ethmoid, temporal, maxilla, zygomatic, mandible, palatine and inferior nasal concha. Suggested: 'Not every skull bone is flat: the curved plates of the braincase (frontal, parietal, occipital) are flat, but the complex bones of the face and cranial floor, such as the sphenoid, ethmoid, maxilla and mandible, are irregular.'

Hyaline (articular) cartilage covers MOST synovial joint surfaces, not all. The temporomandibular, sternoclavicular and acromioclavicular joints have fibrocartilage surfaces, and symphyses (pubic symphysis, intervertebral joints) are fibrocartilage. Suggested: 'most joint surfaces'. Also, elastic cartilage 'only' in the external ear and epiglottis matches the lab, but it also occurs in the auditory tube and small laryngeal cartilages.

card_facts.quote: Each rib's head and tubercle make joints on a thoracic vertebra's body and transverse process
card_facts.correction: A typical rib's head joins the bodies of TWO vertebrae (its own and the one above, through the superior and inferior demifacets and the disc between). Its tubercle joins the transverse process of its own vertebra. Ribs 1 and 10-12 meet one body only, and ribs 11-12 have no tubercle joint (T11-T12 have no transverse costal facets). Suggested: 'A typical rib's head joins the bodies of two vertebrae and its tubercle joins a transverse process; the costal facets are those joint surfaces.'

card_facts.quote: many fuse as you grow (the skull plates, sacrum, and coccyx)
card_facts.correction: The cranial 'plates' do not fuse with each other: the adult cranium is still 8 separate bones joined by sutures (card 37). The count drops because pieces WITHIN single bones fuse: the two halves of the frontal bone and the mandible, the parts of the occipital, temporal and sphenoid, the 3 parts of each hip bone, the sacral and coccygeal segments, and epiphyses onto shafts. Suggested: '(pieces of single skull bones, the hip bones, the sacrum, and the coccyx)'.

card_facts.quote: the steep, overlapping spinous processes stop the thoracic spine from bending far backward, which protects the chest
card_facts.correction: The shingled spinous processes limit extension and roof over the spinal cord from behind. The chest is protected by the rib cage, not by this. Suggested: '...stop the thoracic spine from bending far backward and shield the spinal cord from behind.'

card_facts.quote: when the five sacral vertebrae fused, their spinous processes merged into one bumpy ridge
card_facts.correction: Only S1-S3, sometimes S4, contribute spinous tubercles. S5, and often S4, have no spinous process or complete laminae, and that gap is the sacral hiatus (card 93). As written, this contradicts card 93. Suggested: 'the spinous processes of the upper sacral vertebrae merged into one bumpy ridge'.

card_facts.quote: cuts friction where two bones meet in a joint, which is why the cartilage on bone ends is called articular cartilage
card_facts.correction: The name comes from its location, not from its low friction ('articular' = at an articulation, a joint). Suggested: '...cuts friction where two bones meet; because it covers the articulating (joint) surface, it is called articular cartilage.'

card_facts.quote: Four skull bones contain air-filled sinuses
card_facts.correction: These four hold the PARANASAL sinuses. The temporal bone also has air spaces: the mastoid air cells (the manual itself says 'The mastoid process of the temporal bone also contains a sinus') and the middle-ear cavity. Suggested: 'Four skull bones contain the paranasal sinuses'. The cloze answers are fine.

card_facts.quote: right where the nerves headed for the eye and face have to leave the skull
card_facts.correction: True for the optic canal (optic nerve and ophthalmic artery), rotundum (V2) and ovale (V3). But the foramen spinosum's main occupant is the middle meningeal ARTERY, which enters the skull. Suggested: '...where the nerves for the eye and face exit and the middle meningeal artery enters.'

card_facts.quote: Atlas, the Titan who held up the world
card_facts.correction: In Greek myth Atlas holds up the sky (the heavens); the globe on his shoulders comes from later art. Many textbooks repeat 'world', so this is minor. Suggested: 'the Titan who held up the heavens'.
Minor. Canaliculi are well under 1 micrometre wide, roughly 100x thinner than a hair. Suggested: 'these microscopic channels'.

card_facts.quote: the sternum starts as separate pieces that fuse over time
card_facts.correction: Optional nuance: the cloze answer 'three fused bones' is what the slides and manual teach, so keep it. In reality the body forms from 4 fused sternebrae, the xiphoid fuses late (around 40), and the manubrium-body (manubriosternal) joint stays an unfused cartilaginous joint in most adults. No change is needed for the lab.

io_facts.quote: c11 = 'Pedicle' (lateral view; printed label on the slide figure)
io_facts.correction: On the slide figure, the 'Pedicle' leader line ends on the tip of the TRANSVERSE PROCESS, on the rim next to the transverse costal facet, not on the pedicle. In a side view the pedicle is the short bar between the superior and inferior vertebral notches, just behind the superior costal facet. The card teaches the wrong spot. Either drop c11, or keep it and add to the Back: 'Heads-up: this figure's Pedicle pointer is misplaced (it sits on the transverse process). The real pedicle is the bar between the two vertebral notches.'

Key #11's leader lines end on the INSIDE of the occipital bone (posterior cranial fossa of the painted model). The ridges there are the grooves for the transverse sinuses and the internal occipital protuberance. Nuchal lines are on the OUTER surface; the skull-from-below plate (skull_inferior c3) labels the superior nuchal line correctly. Keep the lab's answer for the practical, but add a Back note, or drop c14.

The chin points to the viewer's RIGHT, and the far ramus shows its inner surface with the mandibular foramen. So this is the mandible's right side, seen obliquely from above. Suggested header: 'Mandible (lab model), from the right side'.
In the left panel the face points to the viewer's right, so it is a RIGHT lateral view. Suggested: 'skull from the right side (left panel) and the cranial floor seen from above (right panel)'.

io_facts.quote: the sutures are named for where they run
io_facts.correction: The names describe shape or plane, not location. Coronal: in the coronal plane (corona = crown). Sagittal: in the midsagittal plane (sagitta = arrow). Lambdoid: shaped like the Greek letter lambda. Squamous: along the scale-like (squama) part of the temporal bone. The bone pairs the card lists are all correct. Suggested lead-in: 'the sutures and the bones they join:'.

io_facts.quote: the lacrimal fossa drains tears into the nasal cavity
io_facts.correction: The lacrimal fossa is a groove that HOLDS the lacrimal sac. Tears drain from the sac down the nasolacrimal duct (through the nasolacrimal canal) into the nasal cavity. The manual's own 'a small hole' wording is also loose. Suggested: 'the lacrimal fossa holds the lacrimal sac, which drains tears down into the nasal cavity'.

io_facts.quote: optic canal — optic nerve · ... · foramen magnum — spinal cord
io_facts.correction: Correct at intro level, but two entries leave out major contents while the other entries list vessels. Optic canal: optic nerve AND ophthalmic artery. Foramen magnum: the medulla/spinal cord junction, plus the vertebral arteries and the spinal roots of the accessory nerve (XI).
The standard term is MEDIAN palatine suture. The lab manual consistently says 'medial', so keep that for the practical, but a Back note naming the standard term would help.
